record.question:
A security team observes port scans from one public IPv4 address against internet-facing EC2 instances in several subnets. It needs to deny that source at the subnet boundary immediately. The company also requires baseline protection against common network- and transport-layer DDoS attacks and wants to avoid a paid security subscription unless it is needed for those requirements.

Which approach best meets the requirements?

options.text: Add an inbound network ACL deny rule for the source /32 in each affected subnet’s ACL, with a lower rule number than matching allow rules. Use the automatic AWS Shield Standard protections already included for AWS customers.
Add the source address to an AWS WAF IP set and associate a blocking web ACL with an ALB in front of the application. Use Shield Standard for baseline DDoS protection.
Block the address in each instance’s host firewall and enable GuardDuty and Patch Manager. Use the resulting findings and patch compliance as the DDoS mitigation control.
Add an explicit deny rule to every instance security group and use AWS Config to discard packets that match the denied source.

explanation.text:
<<1>> places an explicit IP deny at the requested subnet boundary. Network ACLs evaluate the lowest-numbered matching rule first. Shield Standard automatically provides baseline protection against common network- and transport-layer DDoS attacks without a paid subscription.

<<2>> filters web requests at the ALB. It does not install the required subnet-boundary deny or block arbitrary port scans against the instances’ public addresses. <<3>> can block traffic at a host, but does not implement the required subnet-boundary control; threat detection and patching are not substitutes for DDoS mitigation. <<4>> proposes security-group deny rules, which do not exist, and treats AWS Config as a packet-filtering service.

Shield Advanced adds capabilities beyond this baseline and may be justified by other requirements. A network ACL deny targets a source address; it is not by itself protection against a distributed attack. Preserve required return-traffic rules because ACLs are stateless.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-standard-summary.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/how-aws-waf-works.html

diagram_alt: The NACL rule order blocks a specific source, while Shield Standard supplies the distinct baseline DDoS control.

sources.supports: Subnet-level allow/deny, lowest-numbered first-match evaluation, and stateless return traffic.
Automatic Shield Standard coverage for common network- and transport-layer DDoS attacks without additional charge.
WAF inspects web requests at supported protected resources, not arbitrary subnet packets.

editorial_notes: Substantive answer-content correction: stable choice 1 now uses Shield Standard instead of requiring Advanced. Current AWS documentation explicitly provides the stated baseline at no additional charge. Added cost and subnet-boundary constraints; answer ID unchanged.
Root review replaced the unrelated Route 53/Macie distractor with a plausible WAF layer mismatch.
